 GRANT GAP 
 Senate Appropriations Committee proposes small increase to nonprofit security grant funding
 The draft bill would allocate $333 million for the program, up from $305 million in 2026 
 (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
 Committee Chair Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) speaks during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, DC. 
 By 
 Marc Rod 
 November 16, 2026

 In a draft 2027 homeland security funding bill released Thursday, the Senate Appropriations Committee proposed providing $333.3 million for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, which would be an increase in funding but falls far short of the $1 billion that many advocates say is needed to fully fund the program.
 In a separate bill, the committee also allocated $5 million for Department of Justice grants for law enforcement agencies to protect religious institutions.
 The NSGP was funded at $305 million in 2026, covering less than 23% of applications submitted, with more than $1 billion in total funding requested. The House has proposed $355 million for the program for 2027.
 The explanatory report accompanying the bill includes numerous additional instructions and pieces of guidance for DHS relating to the NSGP.
 The report directs the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide, within 180 days of the bill’s enactment, a comprehensive report on the 2024, 2025 and 2026 grant application cycles and recipients, information that has in some cases been withheld from Congress, and to provide annual reports going forward.
 The report expresses concerns about “discrepancies in guidance and implementation” of the program across different states, as well as to ensure that any conditions applied to the program “are tailored to the security purposes of the program and are clearly communicated to applicants in advance of the application period” — a response to the Trump administration’s conditions on the program relating to cooperating with immigration enforcement and eliminating diversity, equity and inclusion programming.
 It also expresses concerns about delays that have plagued the program for the past two years. “FEMA is directed to prioritize the timely review of applications, prompt obligation of awarded funds, and expeditious reimbursement and drawdown processes so that at-risk institutions can implement urgently needed security enhancements without unnecessary delay,” the report states, instructing FEMA to ensure that reimbursement requests are processed within 90 days.
 It encourages DHS to use NSGP grants to help with threat detection and response systems to communicate and share information with law enforcement and first respondents. And it instructs FEMA to clarify that there are “no caps or limitations” on the use of grant funding for security personnel — a gap that has until now blocked institutions from using funding to pay full-time staff security or off-duty police officers. It directs FEMA to publish a list of all eligible expenses and equipment under the program.
 It directs FEMA to brief the committee within 90 days of the bill’s enactment on how it is streamlining application processing, clarifying guidance, speeding up the distribution of funds and regularizing application timing.
 It further instructs FEMA to report to the committee within 120 days on staffing and administration of the program, including whether current staffing levels are sufficient to administer the program and assist grantees.
 Several of the provisions in the report are pulled from the bipartisan Jewish American Security Act, which includes various administrative improvements and modifications to the NSGP.
 The report also instructs DHS to provide the committee with a report on its progress in fulfilling its commitments under the Biden-era National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism.
 “For a synagogue, Jewish school or community center, a security grant can mean the difference between life and death. We appreciate the Senate Appropriations Committee’s recognition of the importance of the Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP) in its FY2027 funding bill,” Lauren Wolman, the Anti-Defamation League’s senior director of government relations and strategy, told Jewish Insider in a statement. “Yet demand continues to outpace available resources, leaving too many at-risk institutions without that opportunity. As government funding negotiations continue, we urge lawmakers in both parties to make increased NSGP funding a priority.” 
 The Jewish Federations of North America praised the Senate proposal while calling for it to be increased further.
 “Our community is extremely grateful for Congress’s actions supporting the security of Jewish and other faith communities through the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, but we also know that the need has far outpaced the funding,” JFNA CEO Eric Fingerhut said in a statement that also highlighted previous shortfalls and the Jewish community’s call for $1 billion.
 Orthodox Union Advocacy Center executive director Nathan Diament said that he “welcomes” the allocations. “These are critical programs and the proposals are an important step. We will be working with allies to boost these funding levels and finalize these bills,” he said. 
 Rabbi A.D. Motzen, national director of government affairs for Agudath Israel of America, offered a similar response.
 “Agudath Israel welcomes the proposed increase to the NSGP by the Senate Appropriations Committee,” Motzen said. “While we hope that Congress will move closer to fulfilling the more than $1 billion in requests, the $333 million represents a 10% increase over last year and every dollar represents an important tool in protecting our vulnerable nonprofits.”
